topic: The Vital Role of Honey Bees in Agriculture

text.content: When most people think of honey bees, they only think of the sweet, sticky honey that the insects produce. However, these small bugs perform a much more important job for the planet. As bees fly from flower to flower searching for sweet nectar, they accidentally carry yellow dust on their bodies. This process of moving dust between flowers allows plants to grow fruits and vegetables. This vital natural process is known as pollination.

Without the hard work of these insects, the human diet would be extremely boring and unhealthy. Bees are responsible for helping apples, almonds, broccoli, and cherries grow. In fact, scientists estimate that one out of every three bites of food humans eat depends entirely on bees. Because farmers rely on these insects to grow their crops, the global economic value of bees is estimated to be over 15 billion dollars every year.

Inside a beehive, every insect has a very specific job. Most of the insects in the hive are females who clean the nest, feed the babies, and fly outside to collect food. The few male bees stay inside and wait to mate. However, the entire hive revolves around a single, large female who lays thousands of eggs every single day. This vitally important insect is known as the Queen bee.

Unfortunately, bee populations around the world have been dying in large numbers over the last twenty years. Beekeepers regularly open their boxes and find that all the adult insects have completely disappeared, leaving the babies behind to die. Scientists believe this is caused by a dangerous combination of toxic farming chemicals, tiny diseases, and a loss of natural flowers. This sudden and mysterious disappearance of adult bees is known as Colony Collapse Disorder.

To protect the global food supply, humans must change the way they treat the environment. Many farmers are beginning to use fewer toxic chemicals on their crops to keep the insects safe. Furthermore, regular people can help by planting natural, colorful wildflowers in their own gardens to provide healthy food for the insects. If we protect these tiny creatures, we also protect the future of human farming.
